title: Should You Really Give Fs During A Pandemic? https://smartclassroommanagement.com/2020/12/12/should-you-really-give-fs-during-a-pandemic/
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Responding to a teacher who announced he'd stop giving failing grades during the pandemic, Linsin argues that removing the possibility of failure is a disservice dressed up as compassion. He contends it sends students the message they're incapable of overcoming difficulty, reveals a lack of faith in their ability rather than genuine support, and is often motivated more by the teacher's desire for public praise than by student welfare. He argues it's also unfair to tough-minded students who refuse handouts and demoralizing for those already facing hidden hardships, and that removing standards causes disengaged students to check out entirely rather than rise to a challenge. His alternative to lowering standards is active support — flexible deadlines, direct help, and genuine problem-solving — paired with holding the bar itself firmly in place, arguing that true compassion means giving every student an equal opportunity to do the hard work, not exempting them from it.
points: Removing the possibility of failing grades is argued to send students the damaging message that they're incapable of overcoming difficulty.
Universally passing grades are framed as revealing a lack of faith in students rather than genuine compassion for them.
The motive for lowering standards is described as often serving the teacher's public image more than the students themselves.
Removing standards is said to demoralize tough-minded students who reject handouts while causing disengaged students to check out entirely.
The recommended alternative is active support — flexible deadlines, direct help, real problem-solving — paired with keeping standards firmly in place.
quotes: But removing the bare minimum standard is a mistake that does a disservice to the very students he’s trying to help.
Removing the possibility of failure sends the message to students that they’re incapable of overcoming difficulties. They’re not good enough or tough enough or resourceful enough to find a way.
Ensuring everyone a passing grade proves to them that you don’t believe in them. You don’t think they can do it and therefore must give them a free pass.
For the tough-minded students who would rather crawl through broken glass than get a handout, pulling students who put in no effort up to their level is a slap in the face.
Given the chance, many students in want of nothing, who have few obstacles to overcome to complete their work, will check out along with (just about) everyone else.
Equality doesn’t mean removing standards. That’s inequality, and it leads to horrible outcomes. Equality in education means giving every student the opportunity to do challenging work.
